## Solution

**Setup.** Let the axis of revolution be the $z$-axis, and let the circle lie in the $xz$-plane, centered at $(b,0,0)$ with radius $a$. A point of the filled disk is
$$(b+\rho\cos\theta,\;0,\;\rho\sin\theta),\qquad \rho\in[0,a],\;\theta\in[0,2\pi].$$
Revolving through $180^\circ$ about the $z$-axis (angle $\phi\in[0,\pi]$) gives
$$x=(b+\rho\cos\theta)\cos\phi,\quad y=(b+\rho\cos\theta)\sin\phi,\quad z=\rho\sin\theta.$$
Writing $R=b+\rho\cos\theta$, the Jacobian is $|J|=R\rho$.

**Symmetry.** The map $\phi\mapsto\pi-\phi$ sends $x\mapsto -x$, so the solid is symmetric about the plane $x=0$; hence $\bar x=0$. It is symmetric about $z=0$ (via $\theta\mapsto-\theta$), so $\bar z=0$. Since $\sin\phi\ge 0$ on $[0,\pi]$, the solid lies in $y\ge 0$, and the centroid is $(0,\bar y,0)$.

**Volume.**
$$V=\int_0^\pi\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a R\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi=\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a (b\rho+\rho^2\cos\theta)\,d\rho\,d\theta=\pi\cdot 2\pi\cdot\frac{ba^2}{2}=\pi^2ba^2.$$
(This is half the full-torus volume $2\pi^2ba^2$, as expected.)

**Centroid.**
$$\bar y=\frac{1}{V}\int_0^\pi\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a R\sin\phi\cdot R\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi=\frac{1}{V}\Big(\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi\Big)\Big(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a R^2\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta\Big).$$
The $\phi$-integral equals $2$. For the rest:
$$\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a (b+\rho\cos\theta)^2\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a (b^2\rho+2b\rho^2\cos\theta+\rho^3\cos^2\theta)\,d\rho\,d\theta$$
$$=2\pi\cdot\frac{b^2a^2}{2}+0+\pi\cdot\frac{a^4}{4}=\pi a^2\!\left(b^2+\frac{a^2}{4}\right).$$
Hence
$$\bar y=\frac{2\,\pi a^2(b^2+a^2/4)}{\pi^2ba^2}=\frac{4b^2+a^2}{2\pi b}.$$

**Surface condition.** The centroid $(0,\bar y,0)$ has $x=z=0$ and $\bar y>0$, so it cannot lie on the two flat end-faces (which have $y=0$); it must lie on the curved torus surface
$$(R\cos\phi,\,R\sin\phi,\,a\sin\theta),\quad R=b+a\cos\theta.$$
Setting $x=0$ gives $\cos\phi=0$, i.e. $\phi=\pi/2$; setting $z=0$ gives $\sin\theta=0$, i.e. $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\pi$. Thus the two candidate surface points on the $y$-axis are
$$(0,\,b+a,\,0)\quad\text{and}\quad(0,\,b-a,\,0).$$

*Case $\bar y=b+a$:* $(4b^2+a^2)=2\pi b(b+a)$, i.e. $(4-2\pi)r^2-2\pi r+1=0$ with $r=b/a$. The positive root is $\approx 0.151<1$, violating $b>a$. Rejected.

*Case $\bar y=b-a$:* $(4b^2+a^2)=2\pi b(b-a)$, i.e.
$$(4-2\pi)r^2+2\pi r+1=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (2\pi-4)r^2-2\pi r-1=0.$$
Solving,
$$r=\frac{2\pi\pm\sqrt{4\pi^2+4(2\pi-4)}}{2(2\pi-4)}=\frac{\pi\pm\sqrt{\pi^2+2\pi-4}}{2\pi-4}.$$
Taking the $+$ sign (so that $r>1$):
$$\boxed{\dfrac{b}{a}=\dfrac{\pi+\sqrt{\pi^2+2\pi-4}}{2\pi-4}\approx 2.903.}$$

**Check.** With $r\approx 2.903$: $\bar y/a=(4r^2+1)/(2\pi r)\approx 34.71/18.24\approx 1.903=r-1=b/a-1$, confirming $\bar y=b-a$. The centroid lies on the inner equator of the half-torus surface. $\;\checkmark$

Writing $R=b+\rho\cos\theta$, the Jacobian is $|J|=R\rho$.

(This is half the full-torus volume $2\pi^2ba^2$, as expected.)

**Centroid.**
$$\bar y=\frac{1}{V}\int_0^\pi\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a R\sin\phi\cdot R\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi=\frac{1}{V}\Big(\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi\Big)\Big(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a R^2\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta\Big).$$
The $\phi$-integral equals $2$. For the rest:
$$\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a (b+\rho\cos\theta)^2\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^a (b^2\rho+2b\rho^2\cos\theta+\rho^3\cos^2\theta)\,d\rho\,d\theta$$
$$=2\pi\cdot\frac{b^2a^2}{2}+0+\pi\cdot\frac{a^4}{4}=\pi a^2\!\left(b^2+\frac{a^2}{4}\right).$$
Hence
$$\bar y=\frac{2\,\pi a^2(b^2+a^2/4)}{\pi^2ba^2}=\frac{4b^2+a^2}{2\pi b}.$$

**Surface condition.** The centroid $(0,\bar y,0)$ has $x=z=0$ and $\bar y>0$, so it cannot lie on the two flat end-faces (which have $y=0$); it must lie on the curved torus surface
$$(R\cos\phi,\,R\sin\phi,\,a\sin\theta),\quad R=b+a\cos\theta.$$
Setting $x=0$ gives $\cos\phi=0$, i.e. $\phi=\pi/2$; setting $z=0$ gives $\sin\theta=0$, i.e. $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\pi$. Thus the two candidate surface points on the $y$-axis are
$$(0,\,b+a,\,0)\quad\text{and}\quad(0,\,b-a,\,0).$$

*Case $\bar y=b+a$:* $(4b^2+a^2)=2\pi b(b+a)$, i.e. $(4-2\pi)r^2-2\pi r+1=0$ with $r=b/a$. The positive root is $\approx 0.151<1$, violating $b>a$. Rejected.

*Case $\bar y=b-a$:* $(4b^2+a^2)=2\pi b(b-a)$, i.e.
$$(4-2\pi)r^2+2\pi r+1=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (2\pi-4)r^2-2\pi r-1=0.$$
Solving,
$$r=\frac{2\pi\pm\sqrt{4\pi^2+4(2\pi-4)}}{2(2\pi-4)}=\frac{\pi\pm\sqrt{\pi^2+2\pi-4}}{2\pi-4}.$$
Taking the $+$ sign (so that $r>1$):
$$\boxed{\dfrac{b}{a}=\dfrac{\pi+\sqrt{\pi^2+2\pi-4}}{2\pi-4}\approx 2.903.}$$

**Check.** With $r\approx 2.903$: $\bar y/a=(4r^2+1)/(2\pi r)\approx 34.71/18.24\approx 1.903=r-1=b/a-1$, confirming $\bar y=b-a$. The centroid lies on the inner equator of the half-torus surface. $\;\checkmark$
